title: Which model should you try first?
summary: Choose a tool that can read your input and give you the kind of result you need.

intro.what: One AI can read a movie. Another can study still pictures. Some tools can edit the files in your app. Start with the job you want done.
intro.features: A short trial lets you check speed, cost and results. Keep the same files and rules when you compare tools.
intro.exchange: Test two helpers on the same fake mail errors. Count the labels each gets right.
intro.m365: Use the same meeting note to check whether each tool keeps the one firm deadline.
intro.developer: Ask two coding helpers to add the same button. Press the button in both apps.
sources: Google · Gemini models and supported media

sections.title: Pick a test with an answer key
paragraphs: Choose a task you can check in a minute. Pick one easy example and one with a catch. These are starting points for your own test.
sources: Google · Gemini models and supported media

rows: Find the frame where a sign changes
A video-reading Google model can take a clip. Claude can inspect still frames you pick.
Play that part of the clip. A still frame can miss a quick change.
Mix in a blank note. Count correct labels.

Try {{model.google.neon.name}}, {{model.claude.sonnet.name}} or {{model.openai.sol.name}}. For a missed exception, try {{model.google.carbon.name}}, {{model.claude.opus.name}} or {{model.openai.astra.name}}.
Point to the exact line that gives each exception.
Try Antigravity, Claude Code or Codex on the same practice folder.
Start on the home page and try both a good input and a blank one.

sections.title: Match the proof to the question
paragraphs: For a rule, you need the exact words and the date. Gemini Notebook can use selected sources. Claude Projects can keep a set of files. ChatGPT can work with files you provide. For a count, you need the rows and the math. “When does the rule start?” calls for a sentence. “How many visits came after that date?” calls for a count you can repeat.

title: Read the price of an AI answer
summary: Learn what a price row means before you compare two bills.

intro.what: An API price tells you what an app pays to send or receive an amount of text. A token is one piece of that text.
intro.features: The table gives sample standard rates. A request can also use thinking tokens or paid tools. A chat subscription has its own rules.
intro.exchange: Try one batch of fake mail notes and count how many were sorted correctly.
intro.m365: Price the reports your team could actually use after reading them.
intro.developer: Count what it costs a game helper to give ten hints that match the rules.

sections.title: Read a price row
paragraphs: These base rates are US dollars per million tokens of ordinary text sent in or written back. The two numbers can be different. For 10,000 input tokens, take one hundredth of the input rate. For 2,000 output tokens, take two thousandths of the output rate. Add those two costs. Check discounts, tool fees and the length of your input on the vendor’s price page.

sections.title: Count the wins
paragraphs: Try this pretend game. Model A spends 6 cents to give three useful hints. Model B spends 8 cents to give eight useful hints. Divide each bill by the number of hints that helped. A costs 2 cents per useful hint. B costs 1 cent. Add the cost of bad guesses and repeat tries to find out what the whole job costs.

exercise.prompt: A new run costs 12 cents and gives four useful clues. How much did one useful clue cost?
answer: 12 divided by 4 is 3 cents. Keep a tally of useful clues so you can do the same check on your own runs.

title: Make a picture you can actually use
summary: Choose a print, a cut line or a movie, then test the file for that job.

intro.what: A media tool can make a picture, a sound or a clip. The app that uses the result needs a file it can read.
intro.features: An SVG stores drawing shapes. A photo stores dots of color. A movie needs a series of pictures that play in order.
intro.exchange: Make a simple diagram of a pretend mail flow. Check that the arrows point the right way.
intro.m365: Make a picture for a sample training slide. Check the caption at normal size.
intro.developer: Make an icon for a game. Test it as a small button before making more artwork.
sources: Adobe · generating video from reference frames

sections.title: Choose a shape or a photo
paragraphs: For a cutout, ask for a single closed outline of a whistle with no words. Open the SVG and check its size. For a print, ask for a photo-style whistle with space for text. For a six-inch by four-inch print at 300 dots per inch, you need 1,800 by 1,200 pixels. Add any exact lettering in a tool where you can edit it.

sections.title: Plan one moving shot
paragraphs: Use a picture of a game token as your starting frame. Ask for one slow camera move while the token stays still. Firefly can use a first frame and, where supported, a last frame. Google and {{model.xai.imagine.name}} have video tools too. Watch the start, middle and end. If the token changes color halfway through, revise that part of the prompt.
sources: Adobe · generating video from reference frames

sections.title: Listen through the real speaker
paragraphs: For narration, give the tool the exact script. For a transcript, give it a recording and check the words. For music, describe the mood and the ending. Try playing a spoken game hint over a short music clip. Listen on your iPad. If a drum hides the score, turn the music down and listen again.

title: Try the same puzzle with three helpers
summary: A made-up parking rule gives you an answer key for a fair test.

intro.what: A fair test gives every helper the same words and the same facts. You decide how to score the answers before you see them.
intro.features: You can repeat a run, change one rule and count what each helper gets right. That is one way to tell whether a change helped.
intro.exchange: Give three helpers the same pretend inbox rule. Keep the answer key on paper.
intro.m365: Use the same meeting invite to test which helper finds a missing end time.
intro.developer: Change one game rule. See whether all three helpers update the score in the right way.

sections.title: Use the same question
paragraphs: Start fresh chats in Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT. Give each this rule: “Charge $2 for each started hour, up to $10 per visit. A visit that starts at 6 p.m. or later costs $4 for the whole visit.” Ask about three visits on one day. A runs from 5:30 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. B runs from 6 p.m. to 6:20 p.m. C runs from 9:05 a.m. to 3:10 p.m. Ask for the charge and the rule used.

sections.title: Score what you can check
paragraphs: Give a point for each correct charge. Give one more point if the answer uses the start time for the evening rule. Give one more if it spots the daily limit. A total of five points is possible. Record the time the answer took in a separate box.

rows: It starts before 6 p.m. Two hours and 15 minutes use three started hours.
It starts right at 6 p.m., so the evening rule applies.
Six hours and five minutes use seven started hours. The $14 total stops at the $10 limit.

sections.title: Change just one word
paragraphs: Change “starts” to “ends” in the evening rule. Ask again. A now costs $4 because it ends after 6 p.m. If a helper keeps its old answer, ask it to show the part of the new rule it used. The changed rule tells you more than simply asking the same question again.
